newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia streamlines logging regulations.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia streamlines logging regulations.

text.p: British Columbia announced on Monday changes to its logging regulations that it said would streamline bureaucracy and reduce costs for forestry companies without compromising environmental standards.
Forest Minister David Zirnhelt said the revisions to the Forest Practices Code would reduce paperwork and enable forest officers to spend more time in the field.
"We have consulted widely and these initial changes will make regulations simpler and less costly for government and industry while preserving our high environmental standards," Zirnhelt said.

Among the changes were reducing the number of operating plans required to three from six, streamlining the approval process so companies could obtain a two-year supply of cutting permits for each timber license, making regulations clearer and speeding up government response to logging proposals.
The Forest Practices Code was introduced two years ago after fierce protests by environmentalists over what they described as damaging logging practices in the province.
While voicing support for high environmental standards, forest companies have since complained loudly about increased red tape, delays and higher costs.

An April study commissioned by the government estimated that timber costs for the industry had risen 75 percent since 1992. The cost of a delivered cubic meter of wood rose to an average C$86.74 from C$49.57 in 1992.
Of that increase, C$12.22 resulted from the new code, making it the second biggest contributor to the rise after increased stumpage and royalty payments.
Zirnhelt said there would be savings for both the industry and the government from the revisions announced today, but he could not quantify the amounts.
The Council of Forest Industries, representing companies, welcomed the changes.

"It's all positive," said Ike Barber, chief executive of Slocan Forest Products Ltd, on behalf of the association. Companies generally planned to implement the changes but recognized that "the standards are very, very demanding and in themselves very costly."
The revisions would allow company and government foresters to spend more time in the field and give them more time to plan operations.
But many environmentalists were alarmed by the changes.
Paul George of the Western Canada Wilderness Committee told local radio that the revisions were "a sellout" of the environment.
Environmentalists argued that the companies -- unwilling to meet the most stringent standards -- had persuaded the government to water them down.
